text.en: The Mashgiach links the calendar to the Torah reading: the meraglim set out the week after Parshas Shlach, and that is exactly the week the summer travel season begins, so the parsha is a message to the traveler.
Every place a person reaches offers him a choice between mitzvos and aveiros, and his neshamah hears Hashem sending him there even when his physical ears do not.
A tree, a brook or a faucet may have waited hundreds of years for a Jew to come and make a bracha there; through the bracha the tree itself finds life and becomes a happy tree.
The Mashgiach reads the word meraglim as coming from 'feet': all who use their feet to go places are meraglim and shluchim of Hashem.

The Mashgiach reads 'Vayigdelu' as the day both brothers grew at once, each at a different passing: Yaakov absorbing Avraham's kedushah, Esav absorbing Nimrod's evil, which also explains why Rashi's thirteen must be fifteen.
Just as the mitzvos of a tzaddik gather to escort him at his passing, the aveiros of a rasha gather to drag him down, and each passing creates an atmosphere that whoever is susceptible absorbs.

The Mashgiach explains Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya's answer by the rule of parallels: the great opponents of the Jews exist only as the counterpart of a tzaddik of the same level, so they leave the scene with him.
Physical pollution of air, water and forests mirrors the spiritual pollution carried by the airwaves into homes.

Purim may not pass the fifteenth because the waning half of the month is Esav's territory, yet Chanukah deliberately falls when the moon disappears, at night, in the reshus harabim, to bring kedushah into the domain of darkness.

The Greeks' decree to write on every door that Jews have no share in the G-d of Israel was the opposite of the mezuzah, and the Chanukah light answers it by carrying the Beis Hamikdash out into their territory.
The empty cups of the menorah, filled one more each night, are neshamos waiting to be lit until all are lit on the eighth day, the number of Moshiach.
The Mashgiach reads the opening of the Shulchan Aruch, about rising like a lion, as a statement about going to sleep: only one who lies down like a lion, with kabbalas ol, can rise like one.
The animals and earth sinned in the generation of the Flood because each was part of a sinner's portion of creation; Noach's portion, which included Eretz Yisrael, stayed pure and was not flooded.
When Tehillim calls on angels, sun and moon to praise Hashem, it implies that man's good conduct enables them to praise better and to shine more.
Hashem may cause a tzaddik to stumble so that his teshuvah brings thoughts of teshuvah into other Jews.
A shogeg brings a korban because a careful Jew is helped from Heaven not to forget; the very fact that the excuse arose shows a lack of care.

Mesiras nefesh is not reserved for giving up one's life: since life is simply the greatest thing a person wants, every overcoming of one's own will for Hashem's will is the same act on a smaller scale.
Dovid Hamelech, introducing yiras Hashem, defines it by guarding the tongue and pursuing peace; so anything that contradicts those pesukim, however pious it looks, is not yiras Hashem.
The berachah on blossoming trees, made because they were created for people's enjoyment, applies to all of creation: its beauty is a gift for which one must return thanks to Hashem.
The interruption of 'Mah rabu' in the middle of Barchi Nafshi shows Dovid Hamelech so overwhelmed by creation's beauty that he could not wait until the end to praise Hashem.
Reading 'tzafra ve-ramsha' as birds singing by day and insects by night, the Mashgiach notes that a Jew can sing to Hashem both by day and by night.
Looking out at creation can itself be looking into the siddur, since the pesukim one says are describing exactly what one sees.
Hashem could have fueled people with something like gasoline; that He gave foods that are tasty and beautiful is a reason to make each berachah with kavanah.

The Jews' loss of faith right before Yetzias Mitzrayim was not a decline in them but the Satan's last, strongest assault on emunah before a geulah, and the same pattern repeats before the final geulah.
The difficulty of being a Jew today is itself a sign that the Satan senses his end, like a candle that flares brightest as it is about to go out.
Esav's dotted kiss is the model for modern exile: where open hatred failed, friendship and brotherhood draw far more Jews away from Yiddishkeit.
A joke cannot be answered by argument because it is by nature the opposite of logic; one can debate a philosopher, but not a leitz.
People pity someone with a broken leg or a sick heart but laugh at a madman, because laughter is aroused by whatever does not work with sense, and this is the power that leitzanus uses.

Yissachar's two hundred heads of Sanhedrin outweigh Reuven's two hundred and fifty, because Reuven's were in the desert where everyone learned, while Yissachar's arose centuries later when Jews worked the land; the effect of living beside Moshe lasted that long.

Through Sefer Yetzirah's time, place and soul, the Mashgiach maps talmidei chachamim onto Shabbos and the festivals: the supporters of a talmid chacham are like weekdays that think they provide for Shabbos, when in truth the blessing of the week comes from Shabbos.
A mo'ed is where the Shechinah meets Israel, so Shabbos and the festivals, the Mishkan and the talmid chacham all share the name, and Moshe, a living mo'ed, camped by the Ohel Mo'ed.

Just as each Jew's letter lies in the parsha of the mitzvah he is bound to, such as a great giver of tzedakah, Moshe's own parsha is the moadim, which is why the Torah says specifically that he spoke the moadim to Israel.
Moshe's added day before Matan Torah was meant to lift all Israel, at least at the original giving of the Torah, to his own level where the Torah alone is the eishes chayil.
The seven weeks of Sefirah are like seven clean days counted toward purity, and the night of Shavuos is the immersion; its purpose is the avodah of the day.
Pharaoh's real target in 'tichbad ha'avodah' was not the bricks but the Shabbos gatherings where the Jews read their scrolls of redemption; heavy work was meant to cut off their hope.
'Beis avadim' means a house with a way of life: Egypt's culture itself was slavery, work without thinking, and the Exodus freed the Jewish mind from that way of thinking.
Pharaoh feared even the half-conscious sigh of an exhausted Jew at Minchah, since such a sigh pierces the heavens.
The same hard labor that made a European Jew's sigh precious makes an American Jew a sinner, because there it was forced and here it is chosen.
Labor-saving inventions do not bring rest, because the time they free is filled by new forms of the same klipah.
'Melech l'sadeh ne'evad': the person who thinks he rules his affairs is really their slave.
The Mashgiach explains the pull of texting psychologically: a person's built-in shame and self-restraint work face to face, and the screen removes them, so jokes flow that he would never say aloud.
Reading the opening of Tehillim, the Mashgiach says 'moshav leitzim' and 'Toras Hashem cheftzo' are two sides of a divide: a person must stand on one side, he cannot have both.

From the Rashbam on one who shuts his eyes while passing women at the river, the Mashgiach derives that need is what turns a dangerous road into a legitimate test: with no other way, a person becomes a ba'al bechirah; without need, closing his eyes does not save him from being a rasha.

The Mashgiach asks why the yud of 'yarbeh', and not another letter, complained about Shlomo HaMelech, and answers that the small yud is the letter of bitul: even if Shlomo was right, one must submit to the Torah.

A heter given for business, the Mashgiach says, is like chametz, kosher all year and forbidden at its time: the phone is permitted only during the hours it is needed, and the rule that what was permitted for a need is permitted without need does not apply.
The Mashgiach sees the new tests of this generation as a sign that it is being prepared for Moshiach and for the greatest greatness.
Following the catalog, the Mashgiach frames bringing a lost soul back to Hashem as a form of returning a lost object to its Owner.
He applies the rebuke over the one who strayed and was not brought back to those responsible for guiding Jewish souls.
The Mashgiach presents the refusal to say 'it cannot be' as something particular to Jews.

The Mashgiach reads Daniel's three verbs as three stages of refining the souls: sifting out, washing white like laundering, and smelting like silver, where the waste falls away and the pure metal remains.
He sees the modern movements as a single process of borer, Hashem separating the waste from the food: each movement swept away multitudes and left behind the souls that hold onto Yiddishkeit.
Communism was the first true 'kingdom of heresy' in history: earlier kingdoms served idols and believed in something, while minus means believing in nothing.
The Mashgiach identifies electronics as the real spiritual chametz of today, so that biur chametz means removing it from the home, the heart, the head and the soul.
When all of nature is renewed in Nissan, a Jew should not be the exception; the trees reviving and the haftarah of the dry bones show that the renewal of Nissan reaches down into the physical world.
Part of today's test is hester panim: in earlier generations people saw wonders from the gedolim, while today everything is hidden and rests on emunah alone.
The Mashgiach reads the Gemara's case of the river path as a model for technology: whether a smartphone is permitted depends on whether there is truly no other way.
Not looking is not enough: Chazal's harsh title falls on the choice to enter the test needlessly, even if he passes it.
Following Shaarei Teshuvah, the Mashgiach explains that the severity of disobeying a rabbinic enactment, such as eating before Maariv, lies not in the act but in the contempt for the Sages behind it.
The Mashgiach finds a hint that obeying the Sages is the center of the Torah in the Masorah's note that the middle passuk of Sefer Devarim is 'al pi haTorah'.
The Mashgiach ties Hashem's help against the yetzer hara to submission to the Sages: one who belittles them loses that help, and then the yetzer hara truly is stronger than him.
The speaker reads the youth's resistance to rabbanim as the same inborn Jewish stubbornness that kept the nation through persecution, now turned inward by the yetzer hara.
A prison and an army look the same from outside, with uniforms, numbers and orders; the whole difference is whether the person inside feels arrested or honored.
He links R' Mendel of Rimanov's words that the last battle was pushed off by 150 years to the years around 1965, when the street openly broke down and personal technology began to spread.

The danger is not only in what the device can reach but in the attitude: a device used with relish as a 'friendly' family device teaches children to enjoy it, while one used with trembling as a minimal work tool does not.
Where Hashem truly requires a device for parnassah, the one who uses it carefully is a hero on the front, not a sinner; the same act done without need is the reverse.
R' Langer reads the halachic test of a bird that swims against the current as a definition of life: being alive means being able to stand against the current of the times.
Following the Avnei Nezer, he understands 'teaching a son to swim' as an education that keeps a child afloat in the waters of this world rather than a practical skill for sea travel.
He compares the generations to a grafted branch, which lives only while bound to the older branch, and applies it to staying connected to the rabbonim.
He reads the letters of 'nokef' in the saying that no one lifts a finger below unless it is proclaimed above as an acronym for notepads, iPods and videos, computers and phones.
From R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld he brings that zealotry is a double-edged sword whose handle is the rebbe; without the handle one cuts oneself and must hold back.
The Mashgiach reads the tree of knowledge as a 'smart tree' whose fruit were smartphones, so that a smartphone in the home is a renewal of Chava's sin, while women's mitzvos are meant to repair it.
The blessings of Sarah's tent did not stay in the merit of Avraham and Yitzchak and returned only with Rivka, showing that the woman, not the men, is the spirit and kedushah of the home.

The Shabbos lamp that burned in Sarah's tent from Shabbos to Shabbos is the model for every Jewish home: the woman draws the spirit of Shabbos into the weekdays, which the Mashgiach reads into 'her lamp does not go out at night'.
Just as the Biur kept Reb Zusha from entering a house, a smartphone brings a tumah into the home that darkens the Shabbos lights and is the opposite of Shabbos.
